thread.title: The United States' Path To Winning The U.S.-China Trade War - SPDR S&P 500 Trust ETF (NYSEARCA:SPY)

author: Louis Stevens
title: The United States' Path To Winning The U.S.-China Trade War - SPDR S&P 500 Trust ETF (NYSEARCA:SPY)
text:
Source: Chinadaily.com
Historical Precedent For U.S. Trade Wars "A fast-rising Asian power has built up a huge trade surplus with the U.S. and threatens American economic supremacy. Washington is outraged at how this new giant has acquired U.S. technology—often, U.S. officials warn, by theft—and how it has used the heavy hand of government to thrust its companies into a dominant global position. Now a Republican president who won election with surprising support from blue-collar men in the Midwest says that the economic rival had better make a deal, or else" ( Peter Landers of the The Wall Street Journal ).
Since President Trump's inauguration in 2016, I've often considered that he's been emulating or taking pages from the playbook of the Reagan administration to guide his policy. After all, President Trump spent the latter portion of his 30s and his early 40s admiring the actions of the Reagan administration as it aided in the dismantling of the Berlin Wall, cut taxes which enhanced economic prosperity in the U.S., waged economic war on Japan, and contained the USSR until its collapse.
And if we consider modern geopolitics, where the U.S. fights Middle Eastern, Wars by proxy, postures itself in Eastern Europe and the South China Sea , and fears the ascendancy of a communist superpower [China], it's easy to understand why President Trump would look to Reagan's administration for guidance.
In the 1980s, Americans perceived the most eminent threat to be the political, economic, and militaristic ascendency of the USSR. In response, America's best political minds employed a policy of containment , by which a mixture of political subversion, proxy wars, and military posturing ensured American hegemony. Although history primarily focuses on the dismantling of the USSR and capitalism's victories, Japan was also among the top challenges for the Reagan administration.
Forgetting The United States' Victories " The passage of three decades has erased some memories of just how big a challenge Japan was thought to pose in the 1980s."
In response to the perceived threat of Japanese ascendency, U.S. officials used a series of threats and deadlines to urge the Japanese to allow the U.S. dollar to weaken against the yen, thereby creating greater demand for U.S. goods and shrinking the trade deficit that had ballooned to around $100B at the time.
Ultimately, Japan agreed to strengthen its currency , which, in turn, devalued the U.S. dollar, creating incentive for greater investment in the U.S. The agreement came to be known as the Plaza Accord and would set the tone for decades of stagflation that would befall Japan.
Could such a dynamic play out again with respect to the tensions between China and the U.S.? To rebalance the Trade Deficit, China would only need to allow the yuan to strengthen against the U.S. dollar. Additionally, without China accumulating U.S. dollars through their export economy, they would have less leverage in artificially strengthening the U.S. dollar. This is some food for thought which I will explore in greater depth in a later iteration of this series.
Are Trade Wars Really That Easy To Win? On Twitter President Trump shared , "When a country [USA] is losing many billions of dollars on trade with virtually every country it does business with, trade wars are good, and easy to win."
Many have referenced the Smoot-Hawley Tariffs, which further exacerbated major economic calamity, as the U.S. descended into the depths of the Great Depression in the early 1930s. But not so many have referenced the ease with which the U.S. neutralized the growing Japanese threat in the late 1980s; after which, Japan experienced decades of stagflation .
So there is certainly precedent for easy work in politically maneuvering in such a way as to hamstring another country's rise to economic hegemony. But today, many believe injuring the Chinese economy would cause the U.S. to suffer itself .
At this point, it's likely not a question of whether certain pockets of the U.S. economy would suffer in the event China stands its ground and retaliates in response to President Trump's actions. Unequivocally, Trade Wars, in which neither side wants to make vital concessions, lead to financial havoc, as already demonstrated by Apple ( AAPL ) and potentially Boeing ( BA ) in the future.
But what about the U.S. Stock Market and U.S. economy as a whole? Could the average U.S. mutual/index fund investor be the one to bear the brunt of President Trump's aggressive tactics?
Since SeekingAlpha is a site for investors, who buy primarily U.S. stocks, I thought it material to answer one primary question for the first part of this series:
Would derailing China's rise to economic and political hegemony negatively impact U.S. Stock Market performance ? I decided to create a regression model in which I analyzed the impact of yearly Chinese GDP Growth on U.S. Stock Market performance, as measured by the yearly returns of the S&P 500 Index ( SPY ).
Here's what I found:
The Chinese Economy's Impact On The U.S. Stock Market (S&P 500 Index Returns)
Figure 1.1 (Source: I created the regression model using PHStat in excel.)
Conclusion : The Figure 1.1 regression model depicts a scenario in which no relation can be identified between Chinese GDP Growth and U.S. Stock Market performance. In other words, Chinese GDP Growth does not and has not explained the performance of the U.S. Stock Market during the last 30 or so years.
For the statisticians out there, I included the relevant data produced by PHStat. 1. The P value is greater than .05; therefore, we cannot reject the null hypothesis (There is no relationship). 2. The coefficient of determination (r^2: .0044) reveals further that U.S. Stock Market performance is not explained by Chinese GDP Growth.
Approaching The Negotiating Table Confidently So perhaps the Trump administration is taking the correct course with their current aggressive tactics. It doesn't seem outside the realm of possibilities for U.S. companies to simply re-route supply chains into India, or other Asian nations, and issue U.S. debt, of which China only holds about 5.5% ($1.14T/$20.5T) , to another sovereign creditor should the U.S. ever need to do so.
Currency Wars And U.S. Treasurys Without U.S. dollars being funneled into the coffers of the People's Bank of China (PBOC) via Chinese exports, the Chinese would have less ammunition with which to manipulate the yuan against the U.S. dollar.
Moreover, China buys U.S. Treasurys out of its own self-interest; in that, China does so as a result of its imperative to artificially manipulate the strength or weakness of the yuan through purchasing and hoarding U.S. dollars, an activity against which President Trump has been vocal opponent . Dumping U.S. Treasurys would only serve to weaken the U.S. dollar against the yuan, which would, in turn, reduce the demand for Chinese exports, on which the entire Chinese economy is predicated.
To be sure, publicly declaring that the U.S. intends to no longer do business with China would more than likely cause immediate backlash from the Chinese, which would hurt U.S. companies in the near term, a factor the Trump administration has probably considered as they've approached the negotiating table.
The Significance of The Chinese Economy If the Chinese economy hasn't meaningfully explained the performance of the U.S. Stock Market performance, at least according to my regression model, what is its significance seen through the lens of the U.S. investor? Well, the company has provided cheap labor, resulting in COGS declining and margins expanding for U.S. companies. Any anti-globalist would be quick to remind us that U.S. companies have forsaken their own (though not their shareholders) in pursuit of expanding their bottom lines.
So in a sense, China has contributed to the increase in stock prices as they've moved in lockstep with higher earnings. Furthermore, China accounts for significant portions of U.S. companies' total sales, as I illustrate later in this piece.
President Trump's Careful Balance Despite the contributions from China to shareholder prosperity in the U.S., President Trump and his administration likely believe that the U.S. does not absolutely need China, in its current form, to thrive economically. In fact, China desperately needs the U.S. However, the administration also acknowledges that certain U.S. companies have become severely dependent on China's economic growth and cheap labor for their own financial narratives. It is along this line that President Trump has come to balance his rhetoric.
"At a news conference on Nov. 7, he (President Trump) started one answer with what sounded like characteristic crowing about a policy success. 'China has come down tremendously. Tremendously,' he said . 'China would have superseded us in two years as an economic power; now, they’re not even close.' But then he caught himself. 'I don’t want them to go down,' he said . 'We’re going to see what we can do.'”
I can't say for sure, but I'm fairly confident that President Trump understands the extent to which certain U.S. companies have become dependent on the growth of the Chinese economy. His current aggressive approach, however, would suggest that his priorities lie elsewhere, most prominently in reducing China's ascendency through its trade surplus with the U.S.
Two American Titans Could Fall... Temporarily Take, for example, the two largest stocks in the S&P 500 Index and the Dow Jones Industrial Average ( DIA ), Apple and Boeing, respectively. Apple accounts for around 3.37% of the S&P 500 Index, and Boeing accounts for around 9.2% of the DJI, depending on the market cap of each company on any given day.
The financials of both Boeing and Apple represent potential collateral damage in an all out economic war between China and the U.S., and by extension, the U.S. investors who hold individual stocks or index funds could suffer, at least in the near term.
" According to BofAML , Apple represented 20.5% of the tech sector's market value at its peak in Oct. 2018..." The decline of a company weighted so heavily in the U.S. Stock Market would not only cause immediate financial devastation, it could also erode investor confidence and cause further market declines.
Apple's Weighting In Key Indexes, ETFs
SPDR S&P 500 ETF ( SPY ): 3.37% Invesco QQQ Trust ( QQQ ): 9.68% iShares U.S. Technology ETF ( IYW ): 14.57% Fidelity MSCI Information Technology ETF ( FTEC ): 15.16% Vanguard Information Technology ETF ( VGT ): 15.69% Technology Select Sector SPDR ( XLK ): 16.77% Source: ETF.com
China accounted for 19.6% of Apple's fiscal year 2018 total sales, and for Boeing, China accounted for around 13% of total sales during their fiscal year 2017.
If these companies, dependent as they are on the success of China's economy, were to suffer as a result of the Trump administration's foreign policy, the U.S. Stock Market would indeed be impacted in the near term. However, U.S. companies would quickly find a new source of cheap labor with which it would produce its goods. Perhaps this new cheap labor market would become the powerhouse growth economy, to which U.S. businesses could sell their goods, akin to China over the last two decades.
Without Concessions From China, Economic War Looms From my perspective, hamstringing the Chinese economy would not alone significantly and permanently damage the broader U.S. Stock Market, at least that's what my statistical analysis indicates. The U.S. Stock Market is built upon the strength of our capital markets and the multitude of factors that contribute to the strength and growth of our GDP . It's not built upon the counterfeit country that China has become in the likeness of the U.S and its innovative muscle.
Globalists and international corporations with interests contrary to those of the U.S. have published reports in opposition to this stance , but one must always be wary of the intentions behind information. This is especially true when the entity stands to lose money .
Nevertheless, it probably wouldn't be prudent to entirely dismantle the growth story of China through U.S. policy, as the secondary effects might prove to be painful for investors and economies around the globe.
" The mere fear of a recession in a country like China , which accounts for one-sixth of the global economy, can hit markets and create a self-fulfilling prophecy."
We don't need statistical models to determine the extent to which certain pockets of the market and certain companies would be and have been injured. Apple and FedEx have already given us that data.
Additionally, a case could be made for a scenario in which the U.S. harms the Chinese economy to such an extent as to create an Asian Financial Crisis, a case of cutting off our nose to spite our face if you will. The extent of economic slowdown in China currently makes such a scenario somewhat plausible from my perspective, although, as my regression model indicates, this would not necessarily spell disaster for U.S. investors who buy U.S. stocks, except for the few that derive substantial portions of their revenues from China.
Moreover, China, the country that boasts having not experienced a recession in a quarter of a century , could likely navigate the loss of business from the U.S. as it would continue stealing IP from the west and perpetuating its counterfeit economy.
Now I understand that there's more to the equation than what I've discussed in this article. The $505B worth of imports China ships to America , the $60B worth of U.S. goods already tariffed by China , and, likely the most impactful, the large U.S. Treasury hoard that China has collected over the last few decades are nuances to the discussion that must be considered. Each side has economic weapons with which damage can be dealt, and it is worth understanding the economic dynamics behind the possible actions the U.S. and China could take if the Trade War were to accelerate.
At the risk of making this article too long, I will conclude here and save further analysis for future publications. Please share your thoughts in the comment section, and don't forget to follow me for more on the U.S.-China Trade War as well as for stock analysis.
Disclosure: I am/we are long BA, AApl. I wrote this article myself, and it expresses my own opinions. I am not receiving compensation for it (other than from Seeking Alpha). I have no business relationship with any company whose stock is mentioned in this article.
